beats.narration_text: Hi, this is Rohan Vijaykumar, from Humanitarians AI. Digital audio is not a continuous wave. It is a list of snapshots. Today I will teach you sample rate, the Nyquist limit, and the trap called aliasing: a high pitch that pretends to be a low one.

props.command: Explain sample rate and the Nyquist limit for a song. When do I have enough snapshots, and how does a high pitch fold into a fake low one?
output: too few dots: high pitches alias

beats.narration_text: Two numbers, one trap. Sample rate is how often you measure the air. Nyquist is the highest pitch those measurements can uniquely catch. You need more than two samples per cycle of that pitch. Go slower, and the picture lies.

show.event: Footer: faster than twice the highest cycle.

beats.narration_text: A microphone sees a continuous wiggle of air pressure. A computer does not. It stores a number, waits, stores another. Sample rate is how many of those numbers you take each second. Forty-four thousand one hundred times a second is the compact-disc default. Each terracotta dot is one measurement.

show.event: Terracotta dots land on the wave.
Caption: each dot is one measurement.

beats.narration_text: I am going to ask Claude to draw the honest test. A clean sine. Enough dots. Then the same sine with too few dots, so you can watch a high pitch fold. Watch the ask, then the result.

props.command: Draw a teaching sine with dense sample dots that reconstruct it, then the same high sine with too few dots so a slow alias appears. No rainbow palette. Label what the alias is.
output: Nyquist is half the sample rate
too few dots invent a fake low

beats.narration_text: When you take more than two samples per cycle, the original wiggle comes back. The terracotta curve is not a guess. It is the unique sine those dots can belong to. This is the sampling theorem in one picture: enough measurements, and the pitch is recoverable.

Now undersample. The true wave is fast. The dots are too sparse. Join the dots and you get a slow terracotta lie. That lie is an alias: a high pitch stored as a fake low one. A spectrogram of this file will show energy in the wrong place. The high pitch was never kept.

show.event: Slow terracotta alias draws through the dots.

beats.narration_text: Use Nyquist to choose a sample rate, to read the top of a spectrogram, and to catch a fake high. Do not upsample a sixteen kilohertz voice note and claim you restored cymbals. Stretching the list does not invent the missing cycles. And do not treat one hundred ninety-two kilohertz as magic if the source was already band-limited.

show.event: Right: do not upsample to invent highs.

beats.narration_text: Remember the split. Sample rate is how often you measure. Nyquist is half of that. Use it to know which pitches can be stored. Do not hand extra zeros the job of restoring air that was never sampled.

artifactLines: Sample rate is measurements per second.
Nyquist is half that  -  the unique-pitch ceiling.
Too few snapshots: high pitches alias. Upsampling does not undo it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. In Python, sample a two thousand hertz sine at eight thousand hertz, then at three thousand hertz. Plot both. Tell me which plot is an alias, and what Nyquist frequency each sample rate allowed. Then repeat on a clip of your own. Look for a pitch that moved down when you slowed the sample rate.

props.command: In Python, sample a 2000 Hz sine at 8000 Hz, then at 3000 Hz. Plot both. Which plot is an alias, and what Nyquist frequency did each sample rate allow?
output: two plots: enough vs too few
